thread.title: ASML: Extreme Upside Potential - Part 1 Of 2 - ASML Holding N.V. (NASDAQ:ASML)

author: DoctoRx
title: ASML: Extreme Upside Potential - Part 1 Of 2 - ASML Holding N.V. (NASDAQ:ASML)
text:
Background - one good stock leads to another In doing the research for my recent article on Taiwan Semiconductor ( TSM ), I needed to learn about an upcoming technology the semiconductor industry needs to continue to prove out Moore's Law in a cost-effective manner. The technology is extreme ultraviolet lithography, EUV; also called EUVL. The industry is looking for EUV to simplify what is becoming a choke point in modern chip-making, namely the lithography process of semiconductor manufacture. TSM is reporting that it will be using EUV in modest amounts for what is now its latest-greatest node, the 7+ nanometer node, but in a few more generations, probably the 2 nm node, there will be no choice but to use EUV. The era of FinFETs is ending, and the era of simplification of the lithography process is beginning. The cost to TSM and other chip manufacturers per system is going to be great, however, which provides the investment opportunity I like in ASML Holding N.V. ( ASML ) here.
The machinery (called "tools" in the chip industry) required to implement EUV lithography looks to be coming from only one source, ASML. The barriers to entry may be so high that ASML could enjoy this status permanently, sort of the way IBM ( IBM ) became the computer manufacturer for many years - but perhaps more so . If so, rather than appearing expensive, ASML shares just might be on the bargain counter when taking the long view (no guarantees exist, of course).
In this article, I review some key points regarding ASML, and provide some links for interested readers to help you research the story. My investment goal is for 15-20% compound annual returns from ASML over the next 5-10 years, something close to what Apple ( AAPL ) has provided me since 2010.
Please note, I am an investor and layman in the semiconductor field. Any errors are my own; please feel free to correct any mistakes in the text.
Why EUV, and why now? In semiconductor manufacturing, lithography uses UV light to create patterns on coated silicon wafers. This is done in a factory, or "fab," that now costs many billions of dollars to construct and equip with all the tools required for cutting-edge chip manufacture. The pre-EUV state of the art involves using a laser to generate UV light of 193 nm, called deep UV or DUV. The problem is that the wavelength limits the resolution of the patterns created on the wafer. To deal with this limitation, various workarounds exist, but they slow and complicate the manufacturing process. The solution is unfortunately not simple at all: create UV light of much smaller wavelength. Here is an overview of where UV fits in on the electromagnetic spectrum (or EMS):
It turns out there are parts of the EMS that are very difficult to create artificially, and the UV part is one of them. After great effort, ASML has found a practical, though complicated, way to produce a next-gen system, using only 13.5 nm light rather than 193 nm. This is expected to allow much faster manufacturing as the chip industry continues driving innovation into the 2020s, despite much higher up-front and service costs. Note, these systems are quite durable. ASML has been in business since the 1980s and estimates that more than 99% of its lithography systems are still in use, though the old ones have typically been upgraded.
This is the main underpinning of the ASML investment case. Its goal is to work with the chip manufacturers such as Samsung ( OTC:SSNLF ), TSM and Intel ( INTC ) to solve the remaining (and significant) problems with the overall technology, establish and solidify EUV as a cost-effective technology all the way into the 2030s, and thus reward shareholders. ( An article from this May in Photonics Media from an expert goes into these issues in thorough but readable fashion.)
In pursuit of this goal, ASML has acquired a US company, Cymer, and has enhanced its partnership with a privately-held old-line German lens and optical equipment manufacturer, Carl Zeiss. The basic technology of ASML's EUV tools involves using a 2-laser sequence to get molten tin to emit 13.5 nm UV light. This light travels to the mask in front of the silicon wafer. To reach the mask, a series of very high-tech reflective mirrors is required. In the end, only a small fraction of the light reaches the mask. Huge amounts of power at the front end are required to do all this.
Getting this accomplished is therefore difficult. A January article in IEEE Spectrum provides a good and readable overview of the situation. Skeptics about EUV focus in large part on the problems in implementing the technologies as well as the cost.
In the next section, I will go into the two main generations of EUV tools from ASML and how they fit into a bullish financial case for the stock.
EUV tools: no ordinary machinery A news summary from Seeking Alpha provides both some context for the business opportunity, as well as some of the reasons why the stock has been moving sideways rather than up since January. Here are the key summary points from last September's post:
ASML will double its shipments of extreme-ultraviolet lithography equipment next year, according to Nikkei . ASML is entering mass production of the equipment and expects to ship 12 units this year and 24 units next year, which ramps up from 14 total in the past three years. Each unit has a starting price of $119M. ASML holds about an 80% share of the global chip lithography market. Note the price: $119 million, for one unit. This is for the first generation systems, which have more limited light-creation/transmission properties, measured by the dimensionless term of NA (numerical aperture) of 0.33.
One negative I see for this stock is that the projections of 12/24 units for 2017/18 slipped to 10 actual and 20 projected for this year. ASML projects 30 shipments in 2019 and 40 or more in 2020. But it's behind schedule so far, and ASML bulls must hope that this is not part of a trend.
Superior machines, with a higher NA of about 0.55, are planned for volume delivery in the 2022-3 time frame, with first deliveries planned for late 2021 (4 machines to 3 clients). With at least twice the efficiency as the current state of the art machines, their cost is 270 million euros, or about $315 million. That's a per machine cost, and a fab producing logic chips may buy 10 of them.
This sounds like a nice business in which to have a monopoly position.
Some of the details of these EUV tools, and the challenges faced by ASML, are found in a November 2016 post by Semiconductor Manufacturing and Desig n. One of the details shows how advanced the system is: the mirrors are no ordinary mirrors:
Mirror surfaces to reflect EUV “light” are made from over 50 atomic-scale bi-layers of molybdenum and silicon.
ASML has paid hundreds of millions of dollars for a stake in a Zeiss subsidiary to help secure access to the Zeiss products.
In addition to unit sales, service revenue is expected to ramp substantially over time (more on that in Part 2).
The next sections review what we know about ASML's business and what might be coming.
What we think we know for this year Because Q1 numbers are in the rearview mirror, as is the Q1 conference call , it's appropriate in this article to look ahead to the rest of this year and beyond.
ASML's main business this year remains the delivery and servicing of 193 nm (deep UV or DUV) tools, along with provision of other tools and services. Here was the CFO's guidance for Q2, per the Seeking Alpha transcript:
We expect Q2 total net sales between €2.5 billion and €2.6 billion. Our total net sales forecast includes almost €600 million for our EUV business, while we target to ship three EUV systems in the quarter.
Our Q2 EUV revenue forecast is a combination of revenue upon shipment and deferred revenue from prior quarters. This catch-up of deferred revenue was previously forecasted for the second half of the year.
Thus, we have to be careful when we look at yoy comparisons.
The CEO's comments were bullish on many fronts. A sampling of his prepared remarks:
Based on expected growth and current guidance, we expect to see a significant increase in revenue in the second half of the year...
We plan to ship to over 15 greenfield fabs in 2018...
Memory strength in both DRAM and NAND is driven by increasing content, as well as expanding end market applications...
With strengthening demand in both DRAM and NAND, we see significant year-over-year growth...
Logic demand continues to be solid as customers ramp 10 and 7-nanometer nodes...
In DUV [i.e. the current workhorse line], we will increase our factory output to meet the market demand [via increased production at existing facilities]...
In holistic lithography, we continue to see growth across our full portfolio of software and metrology products...
To summarize, this year, we expect solid growth in both sales and profitability. We are more optimistic about our view of the year than we were a quarter ago.
This is impressive. Not a lot of companies are showing this much strength.
It appears to me that ASML is hitting on all cylinders and is in good shape for a slowdown, should one be hitting.
Goals for 2020 and beyond The PowerPoint Presentation accompanying Q1 results summarizes matters on Slide 4, saying:
ASML models a 2020 annual revenue opportunity of €11 billion with an EPS > €9*, with significant further growth potential into the next decade.
Translated to USD, that would suggest revenues close to $13 billion. If we take EPS as being in the range of 9.25 euros per share, then EPS would be close to $11, at current exchange rates.
With ASML ADRs trading around $200 at Tuesday's close, that suggests a P/E based on 2020 EPS of 18.2X. I think that's very attractive if that significant growth potential materializes: the company is in the midst of a good growth spurt. Per p. 163 (PDF slide 170) of its 2017 Annual Report, SEC form 20-F , net sales grew from 5.2 billion euros in 2013 to 9.1 billion euros in 2017, a 14.6% CAGR. However, and better, pretax income grew at a 24.3% CAGR, reflecting improved margins. And Q1 2018 was strong, as well.
So ASML is already a growth stock, not just a wannabe one, and in the market we have, a fast-growing dominant dividend-payer that is also buying back shares is not expensive at 18X projected EPS for the year after next if it has a case for high-visibility strong growth potential into the 2030s.
Forward-looking reasons to think this goes way beyond EUV and includes ongoing demand for DUV systems, ongoing and potential growth in adjacent products, and services.
Next, some summary points before going into more detail for interested readers in Part 2.
Conclusions: ASML as a growth stock with monopoly-style dominance, with lots of risks The risks to ASML shareholders are significant. There are many technical challenges with EUV. There is a patent suit for at least some of ASML's products from Nikon ( OTCPK:NINOY ). Then there is the position of ASML as a primary provider of tools to a notoriously cyclical industry, with relatively small service revenues to provide a buffer to a down cycle. There are stock market issues related to a high P/E, high price:sales stock as the Fed is taking liquidity away; and there are many other risks as the company delineates in its regulatory filings. So, please be careful here.
Understanding as many risks as I can think of, and in the context of a generally conservative portfolio as retirees are routinely recommended to maintain, nonetheless I estimate ASML to have a significantly positive reward versus risk and have added it to my diversified equity portfolio. Two core reasons to have done so follow.
One is that ASML has the dominant share of the market already in lithography systems, and is rolling out what looks to me like a long-term monopoly in the next-generation systems. In what is now the key part of the semiconductor process, this may provide many years of very high sales that also have A) high margins on sale, and B) high and durable after-market service revenue.
Those points lead to the second point, which is the long-term nature of a potential long-term big win from ASML's EUV initiatives. To wit, many things I focus on in biotech are one-offs. A company gets a drug approved, but its success is almost always time-limited, there will be competition, patent protection is uncertain, and so on. It is almost unheard of for a Gilead ( GILD ) to grab a market (HIV/AIDS in its case) by the throat and maintain dominance for what might be almost 30 years. Moving to tech, think of a dominant player such as Amazon ( AMZN ) or Netflix ( NFLX ). There is little to prevent AMZN's Alexa from falling to a better voice assistant, or for Alphabet ( GOOGL ) (NASDAQ: GOOG ) to invest many billions of dollars in a product and price war against Amazon Web Services. The same goes for NFLX in that AMZN, GOOGL, or even AAPL - among others - could use their vast resources to begin a price war against NFLX for media creation and for eyeballs. These are normal competitive issues. AMZN, NFLX, etc. may prevail, but there is no monopoly as ASML may gain in chip lithography.
So, if ASML proves the EUV skeptics wrong, I believe that the stock may well provide alpha for many years from this one product line. Perhaps this is a one-decision stock, though risky. Thus, I think a win from this stock could be a very large and durable win for shareholders in that superior returns could compound at a double-digit rate for years to come.
In Part 2, I will discuss some of the technical and legal risks, why I like the bullish arguments for EUV making the grade, and how some of the sales and earnings trends might play out as the 2020s roll along. I will try to get it out by Thursday, and if not, I hope by Friday.
Submitted Tuesday night, NASDAQ futures down 1.1%.
Thanks for reading and sharing any knowledge or thoughts you wish to contribute.
Disclosure: I am/we are long ASML,TSM,AAPL,GILD.
